title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 25-32
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 25-32 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Human-in-the-Loop, Approvals, Interrupts, Escalation, and Kill Switches”, what is the central focus?
options: An agent that can act on its own against a system that matters needs a person in the loop.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: An agent that can act on its own against a system that matters needs a person in the loop. This lesson builds the control layer: approvals that gate a single risky action, interrupts that pause the whole run and resume it later, escalation that hands an unsafe decision to a human, and a kill switch that stops a runaway system before it does damage.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Enterprise Deployment, Serving, API Design, Rate Limits, and Quotas”, what is the central focus?
options: A working agent is a different thing from an agent many people can use.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: A working agent is a different thing from an agent many people can use. This lesson puts the three boundaries around it that make the difference: the serving layer that decides how much concurrent work the model can do, the API boundary that gives every consumer one stable interface, and the policy layer of rate limits and quotas that stops a single tenant from overwhelming the hardware or blowing the budget. It works through the numbers you need to size a deployment, and it shows how those three layers meet at the same number.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Cost Control, Caching, Model Tiers, Budget Caps, and Spend Dashboards”, what is the central focus?
options: A working agent is cheaper to build than to keep. Lesson 26 stopped a single tenant from blowing the monthly bill in an afternoon; this lesson turns the bill itself into a number you manage.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: A working agent is cheaper to build than to keep. Lesson 26 stopped a single tenant from blowing the monthly bill in an afternoon; this lesson turns the bill itself into a number you manage. It covers the three cost levers in order: caching so you never pay twice for the same answer, model tiers and routing so you only pay frontier prices when a task actually needs them, and budget caps with spend dashboards so a surprise bill becomes an early-warning system instead. A worked example runs the arithmetic on a real agent workload, and the Fortress angle shows a hybrid two-tier stack doing all three at once.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Security: Authentication, Authorization, and Secrets Management for Agents”, what is the central focus?
options: An agent is not a user and not a plain service. It carries two identities at once, the person it acts for and the machine it runs as, and it reaches for credentials with every tool call it makes.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: An agent is not a user and not a plain service. It carries two identities at once, the person it acts for and the machine it runs as, and it reaches for credentials with every tool call it makes. This lesson separates the three systems that keep that under control: authentication proves who is acting, authorization decides what that actor may do, and secrets management keeps the credentials that prove identity short-lived, tightly scoped, and out of the model's context.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance: Data Residency, Audit Logging, and Retention for AI Systems”, what is the central focus?
options: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders. Audit logging keeps an immutable record of what happened, per action, so a regulator or an investigator can reconstruct it later. Retention puts a clock on how long you keep any of it. This lesson reads the EU AI Act's record-keeping article and GDPR's storage-limitation principle, then shows how a real agent pipeline turns its own event stream into an auditable trail.

questions.question: Per the lesson "The Model Context Protocol (MCP): What It Is, Why It Matters, and How to Build a Server", what problem does MCP exist to solve?
options: Bespoke integrations do not scale: with A applications and B tools you maintain up to A times B custom connectors, and MCP replaces them with one standard client-server protocol
Models cannot call functions without a vendor-specific SDK
Agents respond too slowly to be useful in production
Tool schemas are too large to fit inside a context window
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the product-of-apps-and-tools connector problem and describes MCP as the USB-C equivalent that lets anything speaking the standard work with anything else that speaks it.

questions.question: In MCP's three roles, what exactly is the client?
options: A separate machine that hosts the model
A component inside the host: each server the host connects to gets its own client object that maintains a dedicated connection and handles protocol messages
The remote program that exposes tools and data
The end user's browser session
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that the client is not a separate machine but a component inside the host, created once per server connection, while the server is the program providing context and capabilities regardless of where it runs.

questions.question: The lesson lists the things an MCP server can expose. Which set does it name?
options: Tools, prompts, and webhooks
Resources, prompts, and transports
Tools, resources, and prompts
Tools, resources, and sessions
questions.explanation: The lesson names tools, resources, and prompts as the three things a server can expose, while transports are the message carriers and webhooks are not an MCP primitive.

questions.question: Per the lesson "MCP Deep Dive: Tools, Resources, Prompts, and Auth", how do tools and resources differ in who controls them?
options: The model decides when to call a tool, while the application decides which resources to place in front of the model
The application calls tools on a schedule, while the model requests resources
Both are model-controlled, and the only difference is the data format
Resources are write operations and tools are read operations
questions.explanation: The lesson frames tools as the model-controlled primitive, where the model decides what to invoke, and resources as application-controlled context, where the application decides what the model gets to read.

questions.question: The lesson says a tool's name and description carry the decision. Which description actually serves the question the model is asking?
options: "Handles database operations"
"Execute a read-only SQL query and return results as JSON"
"Database tool, see the internal wiki for details"
"Utility function used by the platform team"
questions.explanation: The lesson says the description must answer why the model would use the tool and what it returns, and it contrasts a description that tells the model when the tool fits with one that tells it nothing.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about MCP sampling?
options: Sampling is the recommended way to give a server a model in the current spec revision
Sampling lets a server hold its own provider credentials permanently
Sampling let a server borrow the client's model instead of holding its own API keys, and it is deprecated as of the 2026-07-28 spec revision in favor of direct LLM provider API integration
Sampling is the mechanism that authorizes a remote server with OAuth 2.1
questions.explanation: The lesson says SEP-2577 moved inference out of the protocol and marked sampling deprecated as of the 2026-07-28 revision, while noting that existing servers may still rely on it.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building your first enterprise agent: project setup, end to end", what is the single biggest setup mistake?
options: Starting with a vague ambition and letting the scope grow to fill the empty repository
Choosing a framework before picking a model
Writing tests before the repository is scaffolded
Registering too many tools on the first day
questions.explanation: The lesson says the biggest setup mistake is starting from a vague ambition and letting scope grow to fill the empty repository, when the agent needs a boundary stateable in one sentence.

questions.question: The lesson recommends a root instruction file such as AGENTS.md. What job does that file do?
options: It stores the agent's API keys and secrets
It carries the project overview, the exact build, test, lint, and run commands, and the non-negotiable rules, so a person or tool can operate the project without a hand-off briefing
It replaces the test suite for early projects
It logs every prompt the agent sends for later auditing
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the root instruction file the contract that lets any tool or person operate the project, carrying the overview, the exact commands, and the non-negotiable rules rather than being documentation written for its own sake.

questions.question: The lesson says two things must be settled before you scaffold the project. Which pair does it name?
options: The model provider and the hosting region
The prompt wording and the token budget
What the agent may do autonomously versus what requires a human, and what counts as a good run
The software license and the repository visibility
questions.explanation: The lesson says to write down the autonomous-versus-human boundary because it becomes the permissions model, and to define what a good run looks like so the test set is real tickets with known routes rather than a vibe check.
